Micron stock offers an important reminder for investors
I have a healthy obsession with Micron (MU) stock.
You probably got that vibe this week on my show, Sozzi Unleashed.
I can't find a single company in the expansive universe of stocks I follow that is growing by billions of dollars per quarter and trades on a laughable single-digit forward P/E ratio. (Thank you for the reminder on this one, Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace.)
But hear me out here first.
How the stock market works has a lot in common with how overachievers view themselves.
The stock market is always in a race with itself to find the next big thing. Predict the next big thing, and the trading portfolio could look a lot greener. Overachievers are in the boat, always looking to execute on the next big thing in a bid to keep their overachiever status intact.
For both, it's a vicious cycle that often leads to one outcome: failing to appreciate the here and now.
I think this logic could be applied to Micron's financials.
Micron blew it out of the water on its earnings day this week. Crushed it on every single line item. And with guidance.
The main headline was that the memory chipmaker beat sales and profit forecasts for the quarter, driven by voracious demand from the AI boom. Guidance was also strong, except for margin comments on the earnings call — which may have caused the muted market reaction.
But keep Micron's quarter in the proper context.
Consider this: Micron added about $43 billion in sales during the most recent quarter compared to the year-ago quarter. It added more than $13 billion in sales from the quarter reported three months ago! All of this is massive.
Operating margins exploded in all business segments. In fact, operating margins are over 80% in some segments.
What's more, Micron execs signal tight capacity and higher prices for its products until 2028.
"We believe expectations for tightening supply-demand conditions through both 2027 and 2028 meaningfully extend the industry's runway for strong pricing and earnings growth, addressing a key investor concern that current fundamentals represent a cyclical peak," D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria said.
The stock market is forward-looking, so the race is on to predict Micron's next 12 months of results. Don't lose sight of what this company is doing right now, is all I'm saying.
The same goes for your overachieving self.

Micron Technology (MU -2.05%) once again delivered an outstanding quarter when it reported its fiscal Q4 results after the bell on Sept. 30. The memory maker's revenue and earnings soared, and it issued robust guidance. However, as I predicted earlier, that wasn't going to matter much when it came to how the stock would react following its earnings report, and it wavered between positive and negative territory throughout the next session.
Going into the report, Micron's stock had been one of the market's best performers. It was up more than 250% in 2026 and had climbed more than 450% over the past year. As such, expectations were high going into its earnings announcement, even though the stock trades at a very cheap valuation on the surface. Meanwhile, investor focus has turned more toward the longevity of Micron's earnings power than the strength of its near-term growth.
Let's dive into the memory company's results and prospects to see whether the artificial intelligence (AI) stock is a buy or a value trap.

As one of the three big memory manufacturers, Micron has been benefiting from soaring DRAM (dynamic random-access memory) and NAND (flash) memory prices, both of which are supply constrained due to the AI infrastructure build-out. In fiscal Q4, 73% of Micron's revenue came from DRAM, with the remainder mainly from NAND.
The DRAM market is being driven by huge demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which gets packaged with AI chips, such as graphics processing units (GPUs). HBM has become an essential component in the AI data center build-out. Without it, GPUs would sit idle, waiting for data to arrive, and systems would likely overheat.
Of the big three DRAM makers, Micron holds the smallest market share and derives the least amount of its memory revenue from HBM. However, this has actually benefited the company, as conventional DRAM and NAND price increases have outpaced those of higher-priced HBM. That said, in fiscal Q4, Micron said its HBM revenue growth surpassed its total revenue growth, and it expects HBM shipments to grow faster than DRAM through 2028. It has sold out nearly all its HBM supply for calendar 2027 with a significant price increase, which it indicated will close the gross margin gap with ordinary DRAM.
Moving forward, Micron expects DRAM and NAND to remain supply constrained in both 2027 and 2028. This is despite NAND industry shipments growing in the mid-20% range and DRAM shipments increasing in the low-20% range. It sees no line of sight to when DRAM supply and demand will become balanced.
Micron has 26 long-term agreements in place, representing $32 billion. It estimates these agreements will cover 35% of its revenue through 2030. It also noted that it has a few agreements that go beyond 2030. With increased visibility, it plans to spend $25 billion in capital expenditure (capex) in the first half of this fiscal year to increase capacity, with second-half capex even higher.
Turning to its results, Micron reported that its revenue increased from $11.3 billion to $54.2 billion, easily surpassing the $51.1 billion consensus, as compiled by LSEG.
By segment, cloud memory revenue soared more than 3.5 times to $16.3 billion, while core data center revenue surged from $1.6 billion in the year-earlier period to $18 billion. Mobile revenue climbed from $3.8 billion to $13.1 billion, while automotive and embedded revenue jumped from $1.4 billion to $6.8 billion. Gross margin expanded to 86.8%, up from just 44.7% a year ago, and was up from 84.6% in fiscal Q3.
Adjusted earnings per share (EPS) came in at $25.11 compared to $3.03 a year ago. That was ahead of the $31.61 in adjusted EPS that analysts expected.
Looking ahead, Micron guided for fiscal Q1 revenue of around $61.5 billion with gross margins of approximately 86.25%. The company is looking for adjusted EPS of about $38.15 at the midpoint. That was well above the consensus for adjusted EPS of $35.40 and revenue of $57 billion.
Is Micron stock a buy?
With a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 6.5 times fiscal 2027 analyst estimates, Micron's stock looks dirt cheap. The company is seeing spectacular growth, but the question is where earnings will normalize, given that the memory market has historically seen very large boom-and-bust cycles.
Despite its growing HBM business, Micron is still the memory maker most exposed to a drop in conventional DRAM prices, and the balancing of the market would hit its earnings power hard. That is why I'd pass on the stock and prefer rival SK Hynix, which is the HBM market leader and gets the highest percentage of its revenue from next-generation memory.

Crypto has reached its “Micron moment”, said Wall Street veteran Jordi Visser on Saturday. He used the term for a repricing that happens much faster than investors expect, as was the case with Micron (MU) shares. Visser added that token volumes are set to go "through the roof."
Visser said on Anthony Pompliano’s show that he coined the term based on his own experience trading Micron. "I expect the stock of the chipmaker to double, even triple," he said. But instead it traded at 14 times earnings growth, he said.
“Every wealth advisor, every wealth management firm, is going to be in a very, very difficult position a year from now. Their clients are going to start hearing about how people are making a lot of money in crypto, and they're going to hear crypto,” Visser said, while adding that "stocks are going to be tokenized for sure."
Advertisement|Remove ads.
The veteran macro investor said token volumes will climb because of tokenization, stablecoin payments, and AI agents. He said agents are key to his view. "If it wasn't for agents, which will speed this process up to make it easier, I wouldn't be as optimistic on it," he added.
He explained that large investors already want crypto exposure. However, their options are limited to exchange-traded funds (ETFs), digital asset treasury companies, and a handful of listed stocks. "It's really hard, but they want to do it,” Visser said. He also added that tokenization will expand the investment options.
Micron's own numbers show why Visser uses it as a guide. On September 30, the company posted record fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $54.23 billion, up 379% from a year earlier.

A look at the revenue trends between Micron Technology and Qualcomm reveal the former's critical role in the artificial intelligence boom, and the latter's recent struggles, ironically because of the success Micron is seeing.
Qualcomm's revenue was experiencing consistent year-over-year revenue growth until 2026. This year, the company's sales started to decline. A key factor behind the drop is reflected in Micron's revenue performance. As Micron's sales exploded in 2026, so did prices for its products. This created headwinds for Qualcomm's mobile device business.
As a result of skyrocketing prices for components such as computer memory, Qualcomm's margins are being compressed. At the same time, rising prices have reduced consumer demand for smartphone handsets, a double whammy for the company.
In an effort to better align its business with the rapidly changing semiconductor industry's direction, Qualcomm is shifting focus toward servicing the AI data center market. In a sign it's gaining traction here, the company captured tech titan Amazon as one of its customers in September.

Contrasting ratings from Seeking Alpha and Goldman Sachs reveal a widening divide over AI infrastructure's staying power
Micron Technology is sitting at the center of one of the more interesting disagreements in tech investing right now. On one side, Seeking Alpha contributors handed the memory chipmaker a Strong Buy rating in September 2026, pointing to long-term supply agreements and surging AI-driven demand. On the other, Goldman Sachs assigned Micron a Neutral rating around the same time, part of a broader note flagging a significant cooldown in how investors are valuing AI infrastructure stocks.
The bull case: memory is the oil of the AI economy
Seeking Alpha’s Strong Buy call came with a price target of $2,463 per share. The core thesis centers on DRAM and NAND memory, where Micron is one of a small number of companies globally that can produce these components at scale. Analysts backing the Strong Buy view point specifically to Micron’s supply commitment agreements, long-term take-or-pay contracts where customers agree to purchase set volumes of memory over extended periods. Micron has secured more than $2 billion in customer deposits through these arrangements. Multiple Seeking Alpha contributors covering Micron in 2026 have cited high gross margins alongside structural AI demand as reasons to stay constructive on the stock.
The bear (or at least cautious) case: valuations got ahead of the story
The Goldman note, published around September 24-25, 2026, flagged that the median forward price-to-earnings ratio for AI infrastructure stocks had dropped from 32x in April 2026 to 22x. Goldman maintained Buy ratings on Nvidia and Broadcom while assigning Neutral to Micron, reflecting a view that Nvidia and Broadcom are more directly embedded in the AI compute stack, while memory suppliers like Micron sit one layer removed.
What this divide signals for the broader AI trade
Micron’s $2 billion-plus in secured customer deposits suggests the company has converted AI enthusiasm into binding contractual relationships. When median valuations fall from 32x to 22x over a matter of months, the market is repricing the probability that AI infrastructure earnings will be as large, as soon, and as durable as the 2025 consensus assumed. Micron’s long-term supply agreements offer some insulation from that repricing, and whether they offer enough insulation is the question dividing analysts right now.

Micron (NASDAQ:MU | MU Price Prediction) reports fiscal fourth-quarter results tomorrow after the close. Shares are up 273.63% year to date, so the fiscal Q1 outlook will move the stock more than the quarter itself.
Last quarter, revenue reached $41.46 billion, up 345.7% year over year. Non-GAAP EPS of $25.11 beat the $20.28 consensus, which made seven consecutive EPS beats. Gross margin hit a record 84.9%.
Management guided fiscal Q4 to $50.0 billion in revenue (plus or minus $1.0 billion), EPS of $31.00 and gross margin near 86%. Management also said the outlook reflects “a meaningful moderation in the rate of price increases.”
The stock’s reaction shows how high the bar sits. Shares jumped 15.74% on report day in June, then fell 32.39% over the next 30 days. They have climbed 14.24% over the past month to $1,065.71.
Consensus Calls for Another Record Quarter
Check the Calendar Before Judging the Guide
Fiscal Q4 has 14 weeks instead of the normal 13. Fiscal Q1 goes back to 13, so the sequential guide can look softer even if the weekly revenue run rate stays strong. On a 13-week basis, the $50 billion midpoint works out to roughly $46.43 billion.
Analysts already model fiscal Q1 revenue of $56.85 billion and EPS of $34.9476. If the guide comes in below those numbers, I’d account for the missing week before responding.
Beyond the calendar, I’m watching three things:
New SCAs: Micron has signed 16 Strategic Customer Agreements. Fourteen of them carry about $100 billion of revenue at floor prices, and management expected about $10 billion in customer deposits this quarter. Each new deal adds visibility.
HBM4 share: Share holding around 20% would show Micron keeping pace in AI accelerators. Management targets HBM share close to its DRAM share, and HBM4 12-high is ramping twice as fast as HBM3E 12-high.
Supply timing: Management expects tightness beyond 2027 and only gradual supply improvement in 2028. Idaho’s ID2 fab targets first wafer output in late-calendar 2028. The longer meaningful new supply stays pushed into 2028, the longer pricing power holds up.
A Softer Guide Could Mask Stronger Earnings Power
Micron trades at 24x trailing earnings and 7x forward earnings. It has 44 buy ratings and an average target of $1,520.76. Polymarket traders put the odds of an EPS beat at 0.96.
A beat rarely ensures a rally. Micron topped estimates in each of its last 8 reports, but on average the stock fell 3.44% in the week that followed.
If SCAs keep adding up and supply stays tight into 2028, a lower Q1 guide caused by the shorter quarter tells you little about where earnings are headed.

Micron Technology earnings preview: AI demand puts margins and guidance in the spotlight
Micron Technology reports its fiscal fourth-quarter results after the US close on 30 September, with the memory-chip maker's latest earnings set to provide an important test of whether the artificial intelligence boom can continue to drive record revenue, margins and cash flow.
Micron has become one of the major beneficiaries of the surge in AI infrastructure spending. Demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which is used alongside advanced AI processors in data centres, has transformed the company's earnings outlook and helped push profitability to levels rarely seen in the memory-chip industry.
The question for investors is whether the momentum can continue into fiscal 2027.
Those looking to trade around the results can do so through spread betting or CFD trading, while longer-term investors can access Micron shares through IG Invest or our share dealing service.
What is expected from Micron's results?
Micron's own guidance for the fiscal fourth quarter calls for revenue of $50bn, plus or minus $1bn, non-GAAP gross margin of around 86% and adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of approximately $31, plus or minus $1.
Those figures would represent another huge year-on-year increase following a record fiscal third quarter.
Q3 revenue jumped to $41.46bn, from $23.86bn in the previous quarter and $9.30bn a year earlier. Non-GAAP EPS reached $25.11, while operating cash flow surged to $25.39bn.
Gross margin was particularly striking, rising to 84.6%, compared with 74.4% in Q2 and just 37.7% a year earlier.
The fourth-quarter guidance therefore implies that Micron expects both revenue and profitability to continue increasing as the AI-related memory shortage persists.
According to LSEG Data & Analytics, analysts expect Q4 revenue to rise to $51.07bn, pre-tax profit to $42.45bn and EPS to $31.61, all over a 100% higher than in Q4 2025.
AI and HBM remain the main growth engines
The biggest driver of Micron's earnings is increasingly its exposure to AI data centres.
High-bandwidth memory is particularly important because AI accelerators require large amounts of very fast memory to process increasingly complex workloads. Micron's HBM4 products have entered high-volume shipments for leading customers, while the company has also been preparing HBM4E for volume production in 2027.
The scale of the opportunity is reflected in Micron's business mix.
Its Cloud Memory Business Unit generated $13.77bn of revenue in Q3, up sharply from $7.75bn in Q2. Core Data Center revenue more than doubled sequentially to $11.52bn.
Investors will therefore be listening closely to management's comments on HBM demand, customer commitments and the pace at which new products are being adopted.
For those tracking the broader semiconductor sector, our trading platform gives you access to Micron and thousands of other global shares and markets.
For Micron, strong demand is only half the story. The other half is pricing.
Memory manufacturers have historically suffered from severe boom-and-bust cycles. When supply exceeds demand, prices can collapse rapidly and margins can disappear. Conversely, periods of constrained supply can produce dramatic increases in profitability.
The current cycle is unusual because AI-related demand is absorbing a growing proportion of advanced memory production.
Micron's forecast of an approximately 86% non-GAAP gross margin for Q4 suggests management currently expects favourable pricing and product mix to persist.
That makes commentary on Dynamic Random-Access Memory (DRAM) and non-volatile memory (NAND) pricing particularly important.
Samsung has also indicated that HBM could consume an increasingly large proportion of industry DRAM capacity. If manufacturers continue allocating capacity towards HBM, supplies of conventional DRAM could remain relatively constrained, potentially supporting pricing.
The risk, however, is that the industry eventually adds too much capacity. Investors will therefore want to know how Micron is balancing capacity expansion against demand visibility.
While the September-quarter numbers will be important, the market reaction could ultimately depend more on what Micron says about fiscal 2027.
Expectations have risen rapidly alongside the company's earnings. That means simply beating its own $50bn revenue guidance may no longer be sufficient to drive the shares higher if management adopts a more cautious outlook.
Investors will want evidence that AI demand is creating a more durable memory upcycle rather than simply producing another short-lived period of supply shortages and elevated prices.
Particular attention is likely to be paid to:
Fiscal 2027 revenue and margin expectations
Multi-year customer agreements are also becoming increasingly important because they could give Micron greater visibility over future demand and reduce some of the cyclicality traditionally associated with the memory market.
Capital expenditure will be closely watched
Micron is investing heavily to expand production capacity.
The company spent $7.1bn on capital expenditure in Q3, although this was more than offset by its substantial cash generation. Adjusted free cash flow reached $18.3bn and Micron ended the quarter with $30.2bn of cash, marketable investments and restricted cash.
The investment programme is necessary if Micron is to capture the expected growth in AI-related memory demand.
However, investors will be watching for signs that capital expenditure could eventually create excess capacity. This is particularly important given the memory industry's history of aggressive investment followed by periods of oversupply.
The balance between capacity growth and demand growth could therefore be one of the most important longer-term issues discussed on the earnings call.
Shareholder returns are another potential area of interest.
Micron currently pays a quarterly dividend of $0.15 per share, but the bigger potential catalyst is the company's ability to resume share repurchases.
Restrictions associated with funding received under the US Chips Act have limited Micron's ability to buy back shares. Those restrictions are expected to expire in December 2026, potentially giving management greater flexibility to return excess cash to shareholders.
With cash generation accelerating sharply, investors may look for an indication of how Micron intends to allocate capital once those restrictions expire.
Micron shares: what matters now?
The extraordinary improvement in Micron's fundamentals has already changed the way investors view the company. It is no longer simply a cyclical memory-chip manufacturer waiting for the next upturn in pricing.
AI infrastructure spending has created a powerful new source of demand, while HBM has become strategically important to the semiconductor supply chain.
But that also means expectations are considerably higher.
A strong fourth-quarter result accompanied by bullish fiscal 2027 guidance could reinforce the view that the current memory cycle has further to run. Conversely, signs that HBM demand is slowing, pricing is approaching a peak or capital expenditure is running ahead of demand could raise concerns about the sustainability of current margins.

Micron Bets on Long-Term SCA Deals: Can It Lower Earnings Cyclicality?
Zacks Investment Research - Zacks Investment Research - Fri Sep 11, 8:40AM CDT
Micron Technology, Inc. MU is taking steps to reduce one of the biggest challenges in the memory industry — sharp swings in revenues and profits. Its new Strategic Customer Agreements (SCAs) could provide more predictable demand and pricing while helping the company manage future memory cycles.
Micron has signed 16 SCAs covering customers across data centers, consumer markets and automotive. Most agreements run for five years through 2030, while automotive deals generally run for three years. Together, the contracts represent about 20% of Micron’s DRAM volume and one-third of its NAND volume.
The financial impact could be significant. During its third-quarter fiscal 2026 results, Micron revealed the SCAs signed so far represent about $100 billion of remaining performance obligations based on minimum committed volumes and pricing. The company also expects to receive about $22 billion in customer deposits and related financial commitments, with roughly $18 billion expected as cash deposits.
The key benefit is greater stability. The agreements are structured as take-or-pay contracts, meaning customers commit to specific volumes. Many also include fixed prices or price floors and ceilings. This can protect Micron from severe pricing declines during weaker memory cycles.
Micron’s recent results show why it is betting on SCAs. Third-quarter revenues jumped to $41.46 billion from $9.30 billion a year earlier, while non-GAAP earnings surged to $25.11 per share from $1.91. This is a massive year-over-year swing, primarily boosted by the ongoing AI-driven demand for memory and storage.
As SCAs expand, MU could gain greater earnings visibility and stronger cash flow planning. This will make Micron's growth story less dependent on short-term memory pricing and potentially more durable over the long term.
MU Rivals’ Strategy to Reduce Business Cyclicality
SK hynixSKHY and Sandisk CorporationSNDK are pursuing strategies similar to Micron by building stronger customer commitments.
SK hynix has finalized long-term agreements with around 10 customers. These multi-year deals are designed to improve supply stability and support longer-term growth. In the second quarter of 2026, SK hynix’s revenues jumped 257% year over year to 79.32 trillion Korean won, while operating profit soared 557% to 60.54 trillion won.
Sandisk is also moving toward longer-term customer contracts through its New Business Model agreements. The company has signed eight such agreements, covering about 50% of its bits in fiscal 2027 and roughly two-thirds in fiscal 2028. These contracts include committed volumes, financial guarantees and pricing structures that can reduce exposure to traditional NAND price swings.
SanDisk's strategy is already supported by strong growth. The company’s fiscal 2026 revenues rose 175% to $20.25 billion, while data center revenues increased 437%.
For Micron, these competitors show that long-term contracts are becoming an important tool across the memory industry. However, Micron's 16 SCAs, covering about 20% of DRAM and one-third of NAND volume, give it significant visibility as it seeks to reduce earnings volatility.
Micron’s Price Performance, Valuation and Estimates
Shares of Micron have surged around 242.3% year to date compared with the Zacks Computer and Technology sector’s return of 18%.
Micron Technology YTD Price Return Performance
From a valuation standpoint, MU trades at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 6.16, significantly lower than the sector’s average of 20.63.
Micron Technology 12-Month Forward P/E Ratio
The Zacks Consensus Estimate for Micron’s fiscal 2026 and 2027 earnings implies a year-over-year increase of 791% and 113.7%, respectively. Bottom-line estimates for fiscal 2026 have been revised upward over the past 60 days, while estimates have been raised upward for fiscal 2027 in the past 30 days.

Is Micron Stock Cheap Enough to Survive Lower Memory Profits?
Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) can look inexpensive when investors divide its share price by the profits of a memory shortage. The investment question is how much of those profits can disappear before the price stops looking attractive. At September 30's $1,065.11 close, the stock was valued at roughly $1.2 trillion. Fiscal 2026 net income of $84.97 billion puts that equity value at about 14 times annual earnings. A low multiple is useful only if its denominator survives.
The new fiscal-year results make this a more demanding question than the usual debate over whether AI needs more memory. Micron reported $133.19 billion of annual revenue, while its final quarter generated $54.23 billion and an 86.8% GAAP gross margin. Such profitability reflects far more than higher unit shipments. It gives the company room to earn exceptional returns, but also gives investors a large earnings base to normalize.
Micron ranks among our 11 AI Stocks That Will Go to the Moon. But where does it stand against NVIDIA, AMD, and other AI infrastructure names? See the full list here.
Is Micron Stock Cheap Enough to Survive Lower Memory Profits?
If investors are paying for durable memory profits, which supplier provides the stronger bargain? Our Micron-versus-Sandisk analysis compares Micron and Sandisk before this deeper normalization test.
How much profit does the price require?
Consider three sustainable annual net-income assumptions, each an illustration rather than a forecast. At $60 billion, the equity trades at 20 times earnings. At $40 billion, it trades at 30 times. At $20 billion, it trades at 60 times. The stock can absorb some earnings deterioration without becoming obviously expensive, but it cannot absorb every plausible memory-cycle outcome at the same valuation.
The bridge from revenue to profit explains why. Holding annual revenue at $133.19 billion, a 10-percentage-point reduction in gross margin removes roughly $13.32 billion of gross profit before changes in operating spending, interest and taxes. A 20-point reduction removes $26.64 billion. These are deliberately simple sensitivities: a real downturn would likely alter revenue and costs together. They show how quickly a low headline P/E can turn into a higher normalized multiple.
The strongest bullish evidence is that management's next-quarter outlook still implies high profitability. Guidance calls for $61.5 billion of revenue, plus or minus $1.5 billion, and an approximately 85.95% GAAP gross margin. That makes an immediate collapse harder to argue. It leaves open where margins settle after customers have secured supply and competing capacity has increased.
Long-side participation broadened before these results. Insider Monkey's hedge fund database recorded 184 holders in Q2 2026, compared with 154 in Q1, an increase of 30. AQR Capital Management nevertheless reduced its share position 16%, ending Q2 with 3,833,728 shares. The mixed positioning is a useful reminder that more holders and lower individual exposure can coexist; those filings precede the September 30 earnings release.
The contracts change the cycle test. In September 30 prepared remarks, management said 26 take-or-pay agreements cover over 35% of estimated revenue through 2030; most revenue with a defined pricing framework has floor-and-ceiling bands. Management expects margins at floor prices above prior cycle peaks. This is meaningful protection for part of the business, but neither a guarantee of today's margins nor complete coverage of future sales.
Cash generation changes the downside, not the cycle
At the September 15 settlement, 27,633,780 shares were sold short, about 2.45% of float, with 1.1 days to cover. This snapshot precedes the annual results and offers little basis for treating the stock as a crowded squeeze trade.
Micron produced $89.68 billion of fiscal 2026 operating cash flow. Its adjusted free cash flow was $62.31 billion after $27.37 billion of net capital expenditure. The word "net" matters: incentives and other offsets can make that measure differ from operating cash flow less gross equipment spending. Investors should use a consistent definition when comparing cash yields across years or companies.
Using the company's adjusted figure gives an approximately 5.2% cash yield on the $1.2 trillion equity value. That is a stronger foundation than earnings alone, though the spending needed to remain competitive must continue through weaker pricing. Saving cash during the boom can protect the next cycle's investment program. It cannot guarantee the current cycle's margins.
Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) needs to be priced against the profits it can retain as shortage conditions ease. The contracts make a severe decline less straightforward than in past cycles, but their partial coverage still leaves pricing and capacity choices consequential. Gross margin, contracted revenue and cash investment will determine which sustainable-profit range deserves the most weight.

Investors may be confused about what to make of Micron's (MU -2.05%) earnings report for the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026 (ended Sept. 3). The company exceeded analyst expectations with both revenue and earnings, delivering revenue growth well into the triple digits.
Despite that report, investors appeared to shrug following the news, and the chip stock rose only modestly in the subsequent trading session. That reaction probably reminds investors of Micron's often-overlooked headwind, which may affect whether they bid Micron's stock higher.
Image source: The Motley Fool.
No matter how well Micron's financials perform, investors live under the specter of the industry cycle, and its possible effects have begun to appear in analyst estimates.
Admittedly, based on Micron's financials, it looks about as far away from a "downturn" as a stock can get. Its revenue more than quadrupled on a quarterly basis, and for fiscal 2026, the $133 billion in revenue reported is far above the $37 billion reported in fiscal 2025.
Also, the rise in costs and expenses was relatively modest, resulting in a net income of $85 billion. That is about 10 times the $8.5 billion in profit from the prior fiscal year.
Unfortunately, the memory chips it sells are commoditized. For now, demand is far ahead of supply, meaning it commands tremendous pricing power.

Still, seasoned chip stock investors know these trends eventually reverse. This means when supply finally exceeds demand, Micron will have to cut production and slash prices just to clear its inventory.
Analyst estimates appear to offer a preview. For now, analysts estimate a 107% increase in revenue in fiscal 2027. Nonetheless, for fiscal 2028, they forecast growth will fall to less than 8%. That could mean the cyclical downturn will begin in the foreseeable future, meaning investors may have to brace for a sell-off sooner rather than later.
This fear has a profound effect on its valuation. Micron trades at a P/E ratio of just 15 and a forward earnings multiple of just above 6. That makes Micron stock look wildly cheap. Still, a 90% drop in profits (a conceivable scenario given past industry cycles) would take that earnings multiple to 150 and the forward P/E ratio to almost 60 at current prices, highlighting the danger of these reversals.
Considering the historical effects of industry cycles, Micron stock is barely reacting to an exceptionally strong report, and analyst estimates suggest it could bode poorly for the stock.
Considering triple-digit revenue growth and a tenfold increase in profits, Micron has delivered hugely positive results.
However, longtime chip stock investors know the industry's cycles, and the single-digit revenue growth forecast for fiscal 2028 could signal the beginning of a downturn. That appears to render Micron's deceptively low P/E ratio meaningless and could indicate investors need to turn cautious on the stock.
That may be what led to a tepid reaction to the earnings report, and investors should take note.

Graphics processing units (GPUs) are the most important data center chips for processing artificial intelligence (AI) workloads, which is why investors have piled into suppliers like Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices over the last few years. However, GPUs require an increasing amount of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) to keep data flowing smoothly. Without it, bottlenecks would throttle the performance of AI chatbots and agents.
Micron Technology (MU -2.05%) is one of the world's top suppliers of memory, and it's experiencing significant AI-related demand across multiple categories, including the data center. As a result, its revenue and earnings are growing at an explosive rate, fueling a whopping 500% gain in its stock over the last 12 months (as of the market close on Thursday, Oct. 1).
Can the rally continue, or have investors already priced in most of the company's future growth?
Image source: The Motley Fool.
Micron just reported a blockbuster set of results for fiscal 2026
Micron wrapped up its 2026 fiscal year on Sept. 3. The company generated a record $133.1 billion in total revenue, a staggering 256% increase from the previous year. That growth rate accelerated significantly from fiscal 2025 when revenue increased by 49%.
AI-related demand for memory fueled the incredible result, and it didn't come solely from the data center industry. Below are Micron's four business units, their fiscal 2026 revenue, and their growth rates.
Data source: Micron Technology.
The cloud memory segment is where Micron accounts for memory sales to hyperscale customers (including companies like Amazon and Microsoft), as well as HBM sales to all data center customers. The core data center business includes sales of storage and non-HBM memory solutions to data center operators.
The mobile and client segment includes memory sales to manufacturers of smartphones and personal computers. This is an increasingly important category because AI models are quickly becoming more efficient, so many devices can now process them locally rather than relying on external data centers.
Finally, the automotive and embedded business is where Micron accounts for memory sales to car and robot manufacturers. The company says vehicles fitted with Level 4 autonomous capabilities (full self-driving) require more than double the memory and storage capacity than vehicles with older Level 2 and Level 3 technologies. Moreover, humanoid robots are expected to use as much memory as Level 4 autonomous vehicles, so both of these emerging industries present Micron with an enormous opportunity.
In a series of prepared remarks to shareholders released on Sept. 30, Micron Chief Executive Sanjay Mehrotra said memory supply could be even tighter in fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2028 compared to fiscal 2026, suggesting the company's revenue is likely to continue growing at a brisk pace.
Micron stock is technically cheap, but there's a catch
The ongoing global shortage of memory is giving suppliers the ability to dictate prices, significantly boosting their profit margins. As a result, Micron's earnings exploded higher by 879% to $74.33 per share during fiscal 2026. That places its stock at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of just 14.7, so it's cheaper than both the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq-100 indexes which trade at P/E ratios of 23.5 and 35.2, respectively.
Wall Street's average estimate (provided by Yahoo! Finance) suggests Micron could grow its earnings to $176.69 per share in fiscal 2027, placing its stock at a forward P/E of just 6.2. But why is a company growing at Micron's pace trading at such a steep discount to the broader market? Simply put, the semiconductor industry has always been highly cyclical, so investors know the recent bonanza probably won't last forever.

Micron and its competitors are racing to build more manufacturing capacity, which will eventually ease supply constraints and put downward pressure on prices. Micron won't be able to maintain its current level of earnings when that time comes, so its stock might be more expensive than it currently appears at face value. Plus, the rising cost of chips and components could significantly impact demand in the near future.
Last Tuesday, ChatGPT creator OpenAI launched a new $500-per-month subscription plan to suit its heaviest users. At the same time, it halved the number of tokens available through its $200-per-month subscription, which used to be its top plan. In essence, the company has increased the price of its most expensive offering by 150% overnight, and rising infrastructure costs are almost certainly the reason why.
A few months ago, a survey conducted by UBS Group found that 60% of businesses were already routing some AI tasks to cheaper, more efficient models in an effort to reduce costs. These models use less computing power, so if this trend continues, Micron and every other semiconductor company could see a gradual drop in demand.
With all of that in mind, I personally won't be buying Micron stock at the current price. I'm not predicting it will suffer a sharp decline in the near term, but it's very difficult to determine its fair value given the potential shift in supply demand dynamics over the next couple of years.

Micron stock offers an important reminder for investors
I have a healthy obsession with Micron (MU) stock.
You probably got that vibe this week on my show, Sozzi Unleashed.
I can't find a single company in the expansive universe of stocks I follow that is growing by billions of dollars per quarter and trades on a laughable single-digit forward P/E ratio. (Thank you for the reminder on this one, Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace.)
But hear me out here first.
How the stock market works has a lot in common with how overachievers view themselves.
The stock market is always in a race with itself to find the next big thing. Predict the next big thing, and the trading portfolio could look a lot greener. Overachievers are in the boat, always looking to execute on the next big thing in a bid to keep their overachiever status intact.
For both, it's a vicious cycle that often leads to one outcome: failing to appreciate the here and now.
I think this logic could be applied to Micron's financials.
Micron blew it out of the water on its earnings day this week. Crushed it on every single line item. And with guidance.
The main headline was that the memory chipmaker beat sales and profit forecasts for the quarter, driven by voracious demand from the AI boom. Guidance was also strong, except for margin comments on the earnings call — which may have caused the muted market reaction.
But keep Micron's quarter in the proper context.
Consider this: Micron added about $43 billion in sales during the most recent quarter compared to the year-ago quarter. It added more than $13 billion in sales from the quarter reported three months ago! All of this is massive.
Operating margins exploded in all business segments. In fact, operating margins are over 80% in some segments.
What's more, Micron execs signal tight capacity and higher prices for its products until 2028.
"We believe expectations for tightening supply-demand conditions through both 2027 and 2028 meaningfully extend the industry's runway for strong pricing and earnings growth, addressing a key investor concern that current fundamentals represent a cyclical peak," D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria said.
The stock market is forward-looking, so the race is on to predict Micron's next 12 months of results. Don't lose sight of what this company is doing right now, is all I'm saying.
The same goes for your overachieving self.

Micron Technology (MU -2.05%) once again delivered an outstanding quarter when it reported its fiscal Q4 results after the bell on Sept. 30. The memory maker's revenue and earnings soared, and it issued robust guidance. However, as I predicted earlier, that wasn't going to matter much when it came to how the stock would react following its earnings report, and it wavered between positive and negative territory throughout the next session.
Going into the report, Micron's stock had been one of the market's best performers. It was up more than 250% in 2026 and had climbed more than 450% over the past year. As such, expectations were high going into its earnings announcement, even though the stock trades at a very cheap valuation on the surface. Meanwhile, investor focus has turned more toward the longevity of Micron's earnings power than the strength of its near-term growth.
Let's dive into the memory company's results and prospects to see whether the artificial intelligence (AI) stock is a buy or a value trap.
$1.2TMarket cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary.
As one of the three big memory manufacturers, Micron has been benefiting from soaring DRAM (dynamic random-access memory) and NAND (flash) memory prices, both of which are supply constrained due to the AI infrastructure build-out. In fiscal Q4, 73% of Micron's revenue came from DRAM, with the remainder mainly from NAND.
The DRAM market is being driven by huge demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which gets packaged with AI chips, such as graphics processing units (GPUs). HBM has become an essential component in the AI data center build-out. Without it, GPUs would sit idle, waiting for data to arrive, and systems would likely overheat.
Of the big three DRAM makers, Micron holds the smallest market share and derives the least amount of its memory revenue from HBM. However, this has actually benefited the company, as conventional DRAM and NAND price increases have outpaced those of higher-priced HBM. That said, in fiscal Q4, Micron said its HBM revenue growth surpassed its total revenue growth, and it expects HBM shipments to grow faster than DRAM through 2028. It has sold out nearly all its HBM supply for calendar 2027 with a significant price increase, which it indicated will close the gross margin gap with ordinary DRAM.
Moving forward, Micron expects DRAM and NAND to remain supply constrained in both 2027 and 2028. This is despite NAND industry shipments growing in the mid-20% range and DRAM shipments increasing in the low-20% range. It sees no line of sight to when DRAM supply and demand will become balanced.
Micron has 26 long-term agreements in place, representing $32 billion. It estimates these agreements will cover 35% of its revenue through 2030. It also noted that it has a few agreements that go beyond 2030. With increased visibility, it plans to spend $25 billion in capital expenditure (capex) in the first half of this fiscal year to increase capacity, with second-half capex even higher.
Turning to its results, Micron reported that its revenue increased from $11.3 billion to $54.2 billion, easily surpassing the $51.1 billion consensus, as compiled by LSEG.
By segment, cloud memory revenue soared more than 3.5 times to $16.3 billion, while core data center revenue surged from $1.6 billion in the year-earlier period to $18 billion. Mobile revenue climbed from $3.8 billion to $13.1 billion, while automotive and embedded revenue jumped from $1.4 billion to $6.8 billion. Gross margin expanded to 86.8%, up from just 44.7% a year ago, and was up from 84.6% in fiscal Q3.
Adjusted earnings per share (EPS) came in at $25.11 compared to $3.03 a year ago. That was ahead of the $31.61 in adjusted EPS that analysts expected.
Looking ahead, Micron guided for fiscal Q1 revenue of around $61.5 billion with gross margins of approximately 86.25%. The company is looking for adjusted EPS of about $38.15 at the midpoint. That was well above the consensus for adjusted EPS of $35.40 and revenue of $57 billion.
Is Micron stock a buy?
With a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 6.5 times fiscal 2027 analyst estimates, Micron's stock looks dirt cheap. The company is seeing spectacular growth, but the question is where earnings will normalize, given that the memory market has historically seen very large boom-and-bust cycles.
Despite its growing HBM business, Micron is still the memory maker most exposed to a drop in conventional DRAM prices, and the balancing of the market would hit its earnings power hard. That is why I'd pass on the stock and prefer rival SK Hynix, which is the HBM market leader and gets the highest percentage of its revenue from next-generation memory.

Jordi Visser Says Crypto Is At Its 'Micron Moment,' Sees Token Volumes Going 'Through The Roof'
Visser said AI agents are key to his view and would speed up crypto's growth.
In this photo illustration, a visual representation of the digital cryptocurrency Bitcoin is displayed in front of a Bitcoin course's graph on January 11, 2024 in Paris, France. (Photo illustration by Chesnot/Getty Images)
Visser said crypto is at its “Micron moment,” with token volumes set to rise through tokenization, stablecoin payments, and AI agents.
Visser said he expected Micron to double, maybe triple, but it rose 14 times on earnings growth.
He said tokenization will allow institutional investors to gain broader exposure to the crypto ecosystem.
Advertisement|Remove ads.
Crypto has reached its “Micron moment”, said Wall Street veteran Jordi Visser on Saturday. He used the term for a repricing that happens much faster than investors expect, as was the case with Micron (MU) shares. Visser added that token volumes are set to go "through the roof."
Visser said on Anthony Pompliano’s show that he coined the term based on his own experience trading Micron. "I expect the stock of the chipmaker to double, even triple," he said. But instead it traded at 14 times earnings growth, he said.
“Every wealth advisor, every wealth management firm, is going to be in a very, very difficult position a year from now. Their clients are going to start hearing about how people are making a lot of money in crypto, and they're going to hear crypto,” Visser said, while adding that "stocks are going to be tokenized for sure."
Advertisement|Remove ads.
The veteran macro investor said token volumes will climb because of tokenization, stablecoin payments, and AI agents. He said agents are key to his view. "If it wasn't for agents, which will speed this process up to make it easier, I wouldn't be as optimistic on it," he added.
He explained that large investors already want crypto exposure. However, their options are limited to exchange-traded funds (ETFs), digital asset treasury companies, and a handful of listed stocks. "It's really hard, but they want to do it,” Visser said. He also added that tokenization will expand the investment options.
Micron's own numbers show why Visser uses it as a guide. On September 30, the company posted record fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $54.23 billion, up 379% from a year earlier.
Advertisement|Remove ads.
MU stock closed down over 2% on Friday. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment around Micron is in the ‘extremely bullish’ zone, with chatter at ‘extremely high’ levels over the past day.
Earlier this year, Visser said that he had made about eight times his money on Micron before selling his entire stake and explained that the easy gains in AI were over and that retail money was set to rotate into other assets.
He has since turned more bullish on Bitcoin (BTC). In early September, Visser said Bitcoin had joined a short list of things that survive repeated waves of change, stating that "there are very few things that survive the disruption of human beings and technology: religion, gold, and now Bitcoin."
Advertisement|Remove ads.
Meanwhile, Bitcoin’s price traded over $85,000, up over 0.5% over the past 24 hours. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment around Bitcoin remained in the ‘bearish’ zone, while chatter dipped to ‘low’ from ‘normal’ levels over the past day.

When analyzing top-line performance over the last eight quarters, Micron Technology exhibits a stronger revenue trajectory than Qualcomm, establishing a clear pattern of quarterly expansion.
Micron Technology generated accelerating quarter-over-quarter growth, while Qualcomm maintained a relatively stable quarter-over-quarter revenue pattern that eventually transitioned into a series of sequential declines.
Given their divergent financial trajectories, investors should carefully watch whether the expanding revenue gap continues to widen between the two companies or if changing business dynamics cause the established trend to narrow in upcoming quarters.

Micron Technology: Tracking a Pattern of Revenue Acceleration
Micron Technology(NASDAQ:MU) primarily generates revenue by manufacturing and selling advanced semiconductor memory and storage solutions to global customers.
During the recent period, it established multiple long-term strategic supply agreements with several major automotive manufacturers, such as General Motors and Ford Motor Company, to explicitly provide essential memory supply for vehicle platforms. It concurrently poured the first concrete for a new domestic semiconductor fabrication facility in New York.
Qualcomm: Navigating a Pattern of Uneven Quarterly Revenue
Qualcomm(NASDAQ:QCOM) primarily earns its revenue by supplying advanced wireless communication technologies and licensing its broad intellectual property portfolio.
During the quarter ended June 2026, it renewed a global patent licensing agreement with Apple to ensure continued royalty payments through the end of the decade, while it simultaneously secured a long-term computing supply agreement with BMW Group to act as the lead compute silicon provider for automated driving systems.

Micron Technology earns Strong Buy rating from Seeking Alpha amid AI skepticism
Contrasting ratings from Seeking Alpha and Goldman Sachs reveal a widening divide over AI infrastructure's staying power
Micron Technology is sitting at the center of one of the more interesting disagreements in tech investing right now. On one side, Seeking Alpha contributors handed the memory chipmaker a Strong Buy rating in September 2026, pointing to long-term supply agreements and surging AI-driven demand. On the other, Goldman Sachs assigned Micron a Neutral rating around the same time, part of a broader note flagging a significant cooldown in how investors are valuing AI infrastructure stocks.
The bull case: memory is the oil of the AI economy
Seeking Alpha’s Strong Buy call came with a price target of $2,463 per share. The core thesis centers on DRAM and NAND memory, where Micron is one of a small number of companies globally that can produce these components at scale. Analysts backing the Strong Buy view point specifically to Micron’s supply commitment agreements, long-term take-or-pay contracts where customers agree to purchase set volumes of memory over extended periods. Micron has secured more than $2 billion in customer deposits through these arrangements. Multiple Seeking Alpha contributors covering Micron in 2026 have cited high gross margins alongside structural AI demand as reasons to stay constructive on the stock.
The bear (or at least cautious) case: valuations got ahead of the story
The Goldman note, published around September 24-25, 2026, flagged that the median forward price-to-earnings ratio for AI infrastructure stocks had dropped from 32x in April 2026 to 22x. Goldman maintained Buy ratings on Nvidia and Broadcom while assigning Neutral to Micron, reflecting a view that Nvidia and Broadcom are more directly embedded in the AI compute stack, while memory suppliers like Micron sit one layer removed.
What this divide signals for the broader AI trade
Micron’s $2 billion-plus in secured customer deposits suggests the company has converted AI enthusiasm into binding contractual relationships. When median valuations fall from 32x to 22x over a matter of months, the market is repricing the probability that AI infrastructure earnings will be as large, as soon, and as durable as the 2025 consensus assumed. Micron’s long-term supply agreements offer some insulation from that repricing, and whether they offer enough insulation is the question dividing analysts right now.

GAAP gross margin was 86.8%, non-GAAP gross margin was 87.0%, non-GAAP operating margin was 82.3%, and non-GAAP diluted EPS was $33.42. Rather than just a recovery in the memory cycle, this earnings result shows AI data center demand pushing revenue to a new stage.
| Core Data Center BU | $18.002 billion (+1,042%) |
| Cloud Memory BU | $16.283 billion (+258%) |
| Mobile and Client BU | $13.114 billion (+249%) |
| Automotive & Embedded BU | $6.824 billion (+376%) |
The Core Data Center BU reached $18.002 billion, up 1,042% year-over-year. 90% / 85%. This was a 56% increase quarter-over-quarter, representing the strongest growth for AI data centers.
The Cloud Memory BU reached $16.283 billion, up 258% year-over-year. 83% / 76%. This includes cloud-focused HBM. It was up 18% quarter-over-quarter, with gross margin remaining flat.
The Mobile and Client BU reached $13.114 billion, up 249% year-over-year. 90% / 88%. Price increases were the primary driver, up 14% quarter-over-quarter. The foundation outside of AI is also robust.
The Automotive & Embedded BU reached $6.824 billion, up 376% year-over-year. 84% / 79%. Up 47% quarter-over-quarter. Additionally, sample shipments of 1-gamma LPDDR6 for Physical AI have begun, which is a point to watch as the next source of demand.
| Announcement Day Closing Price (9/30) | $1065.11 (+0.00%) |

Earnings were released after the market closed (AMC) on September 30, 2026. The announcement day closing price of $1,065.11 was the benchmark before the earnings (nearly flat compared to the previous business day's $1,065.08). After-hours trading based on Nasdaq quotes was approximately $1,065.98 (approx. +0.08% compared to the announcement day closing price). On the next business day (10/1), the stock fell to an intraday low of $1,022.90 (approx. -3.96% compared to the announcement day closing price) before rebounding to close at $1,097.39 (+$32.28, +3.03%), with an intraday high of $1,098.90. The bar length is a reference value that normalizes the price level within the display period.
The first point is HBM price revisions and the narrowing of margin gaps. The company explained that it has completed contracts for the majority of its CY2027 HBM bit supply at prices significantly higher than in 2026. With volume filled and prices rising, whether the gross margin gap between HBM and standard DRAM narrows is the key to ensuring the gross margin of around 87% does not end as a temporary peak.
The second point is SCA coverage and the quality of RPO. SCA consists of 26 agreements, accounting for over 35% of the revenue outlook through 2030, with an RPO of approximately $150 billion. All cases are take-or-pay volume commitments, and RPO is a conservative figure calculated by multiplying committed volume by the minimum price for confirmed pricing structures. The point to watch is how much the amplitude of the memory cycle can be reduced by fixing a portion of volume and price through multi-year contracts.
The third point is that the FQ1 gross margin is the floor for the fiscal year, and investment recovery is the next topic. The FQ1 non-GAAP gross margin is approximately 86.25%, which is explained as the floor for FY2027. With first-half capital expenditures projected at approximately $25 billion (approx. $11.5 billion in FQ1), the focus is on the balance between directing strong free cash flow toward capacity investment and strengthening shareholder returns (from 12/9 onwards).
FQ1 revenue exceeds the upper end of the $61.5 billion guidance, confirming that HBM price hikes and demand for data centers are stronger than anticipated.
Supply shortages persist through 2027–2028, SCA coverage expands to around 50% of revenue, and gross margins remain elevated.
Supported by strong free cash flow, enhanced shareholder returns starting in December provide a floor for the stock price.
FQ1 revenue lands around $61.5 billion with gross margins in the low 86% range, followed by a recovery in gross margins through gradual price increases.
With the Data Center 2 business remaining the primary driver, mobile and automotive segments also maintain high gross margins, providing a broad foundation for total company revenue.
The stock price remained quiet immediately after the record-breaking earnings announcement, falling about 4% at one point the next business day before rebounding to +3.03%. Moving forward, pricing will be driven by HBM pricing, SCA, and the sustainability of FY2027 earnings.
Supply and demand loosen faster than expected due to customer specification optimization (limiting memory capacity) and increased production by competitors.
Increased capital expenditure and startup costs erode free cash flow and gross margins, leading to an adjustment in expectations.
The price floor for SCA is lower than market expectations, weakening the narrative of long-term earnings durability.
Micron Technology's FY2026 Q4 earnings (for the quarter ended September 3, 2026) were a record-breaking quarter, as described by the company, with revenue of $54.229 billion (+379% YoY, +31% QoQ), GAAP net income of $37.701 billion, diluted EPS of $32.87, non-GAAP net income of $38.398 billion, and EPS of $33.42. Gross margins were 86.8% GAAP / 87.0% non-GAAP. Operating cash flow was $43.973 billion, adjusted free cash flow was $33.199 billion, and net capital expenditures were $10.774 billion. Full-year FY2026 revenue grew to $133.188 billion, with non-GAAP gross margins of 81.1% and non-GAAP EPS of $75.52.

Micron’s Earnings Guidance May Look Weak Tomorrow. Buy MU Stock Anyway
Micron reports tomorrow, and a guidance miss could spark a selloff that has nothing to do with the company's actual earnings power. Here is what to watch before reacting.
Published September 29, 2026, 12:07pm ET · 2 min read
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
A Micron Technology nameplate sits on a desk, representing the company as investors anticipate its upcoming fiscal fourth-quarter results. © 24/7 Wall St.
Micron (NASDAQ:MU | MU Price Prediction) reports fiscal fourth-quarter results tomorrow after the close. Shares are up 273.63% year to date, so the fiscal Q1 outlook will move the stock more than the quarter itself.
Last quarter, revenue reached $41.46 billion, up 345.7% year over year. Non-GAAP EPS of $25.11 beat the $20.28 consensus, which made seven consecutive EPS beats. Gross margin hit a record 84.9%.
Management guided fiscal Q4 to $50.0 billion in revenue (plus or minus $1.0 billion), EPS of $31.00 and gross margin near 86%. Management also said the outlook reflects “a meaningful moderation in the rate of price increases.”
The stock’s reaction shows how high the bar sits. Shares jumped 15.74% on report day in June, then fell 32.39% over the next 30 days. They have climbed 14.24% over the past month to $1,065.71.
Consensus Calls for Another Record Quarter
Check the Calendar Before Judging the Guide
Fiscal Q4 has 14 weeks instead of the normal 13. Fiscal Q1 goes back to 13, so the sequential guide can look softer even if the weekly revenue run rate stays strong. On a 13-week basis, the $50 billion midpoint works out to roughly $46.43 billion.
Analysts already model fiscal Q1 revenue of $56.85 billion and EPS of $34.9476. If the guide comes in below those numbers, I’d account for the missing week before responding.
Beyond the calendar, I’m watching three things:
New SCAs: Micron has signed 16 Strategic Customer Agreements. Fourteen of them carry about $100 billion of revenue at floor prices, and management expected about $10 billion in customer deposits this quarter. Each new deal adds visibility.
HBM4 share: Share holding around 20% would show Micron keeping pace in AI accelerators. Management targets HBM share close to its DRAM share, and HBM4 12-high is ramping twice as fast as HBM3E 12-high.
Supply timing: Management expects tightness beyond 2027 and only gradual supply improvement in 2028. Idaho’s ID2 fab targets first wafer output in late-calendar 2028. The longer meaningful new supply stays pushed into 2028, the longer pricing power holds up.
A Softer Guide Could Mask Stronger Earnings Power
Micron trades at 24x trailing earnings and 7x forward earnings. It has 44 buy ratings and an average target of $1,520.76. Polymarket traders put the odds of an EPS beat at 0.96.
A beat rarely ensures a rally. Micron topped estimates in each of its last 8 reports, but on average the stock fell 3.44% in the week that followed.
If SCAs keep adding up and supply stays tight into 2028, a lower Q1 guide caused by the shorter quarter tells you little about where earnings are headed.

Micron Technology earnings preview: AI demand puts margins and guidance in the spotlight
Micron reports fiscal Q4 results on 30 September. Here's what investors should watch across HBM demand, memory pricing, margins and the all-important fiscal 2027 outlook.
Day trading NASDAQ Technical analysis CFD Trading United States
Publication date 2026-09-29T14:18:02+0100
Micron Technology earnings preview: AI demand puts margins and guidance in the spotlight
Micron Technology reports its fiscal fourth-quarter results after the US close on 30 September, with the memory-chip maker's latest earnings set to provide an important test of whether the artificial intelligence boom can continue to drive record revenue, margins and cash flow.
Micron has become one of the major beneficiaries of the surge in AI infrastructure spending. Demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which is used alongside advanced AI processors in data centres, has transformed the company's earnings outlook and helped push profitability to levels rarely seen in the memory-chip industry.
The question for investors is whether the momentum can continue into fiscal 2027.
Those looking to trade around the results can do so through spread betting or CFD trading, while longer-term investors can access Micron shares through IG Invest or our share dealing service.
What is expected from Micron's results?
Micron's own guidance for the fiscal fourth quarter calls for revenue of $50bn, plus or minus $1bn, non-GAAP gross margin of around 86% and adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of approximately $31, plus or minus $1.
Those figures would represent another huge year-on-year increase following a record fiscal third quarter.
Q3 revenue jumped to $41.46bn, from $23.86bn in the previous quarter and $9.30bn a year earlier. Non-GAAP EPS reached $25.11, while operating cash flow surged to $25.39bn.
Gross margin was particularly striking, rising to 84.6%, compared with 74.4% in Q2 and just 37.7% a year earlier.
The fourth-quarter guidance therefore implies that Micron expects both revenue and profitability to continue increasing as the AI-related memory shortage persists.
According to LSEG Data & Analytics, analysts expect Q4 revenue to rise to $51.07bn, pre-tax profit to $42.45bn and EPS to $31.61, all over a 100% higher than in Q4 2025.
AI and HBM remain the main growth engines
The biggest driver of Micron's earnings is increasingly its exposure to AI data centres.
High-bandwidth memory is particularly important because AI accelerators require large amounts of very fast memory to process increasingly complex workloads. Micron's HBM4 products have entered high-volume shipments for leading customers, while the company has also been preparing HBM4E for volume production in 2027.
The scale of the opportunity is reflected in Micron's business mix.
Its Cloud Memory Business Unit generated $13.77bn of revenue in Q3, up sharply from $7.75bn in Q2. Core Data Center revenue more than doubled sequentially to $11.52bn.
Investors will therefore be listening closely to management's comments on HBM demand, customer commitments and the pace at which new products are being adopted.
For those tracking the broader semiconductor sector, our trading platform gives you access to Micron and thousands of other global shares and markets.
For Micron, strong demand is only half the story. The other half is pricing.
Memory manufacturers have historically suffered from severe boom-and-bust cycles. When supply exceeds demand, prices can collapse rapidly and margins can disappear. Conversely, periods of constrained supply can produce dramatic increases in profitability.
The current cycle is unusual because AI-related demand is absorbing a growing proportion of advanced memory production.
Micron's forecast of an approximately 86% non-GAAP gross margin for Q4 suggests management currently expects favourable pricing and product mix to persist.
That makes commentary on Dynamic Random-Access Memory (DRAM) and non-volatile memory (NAND) pricing particularly important.
Samsung has also indicated that HBM could consume an increasingly large proportion of industry DRAM capacity. If manufacturers continue allocating capacity towards HBM, supplies of conventional DRAM could remain relatively constrained, potentially supporting pricing.
The risk, however, is that the industry eventually adds too much capacity. Investors will therefore want to know how Micron is balancing capacity expansion against demand visibility.
While the September-quarter numbers will be important, the market reaction could ultimately depend more on what Micron says about fiscal 2027.
Expectations have risen rapidly alongside the company's earnings. That means simply beating its own $50bn revenue guidance may no longer be sufficient to drive the shares higher if management adopts a more cautious outlook.
Investors will want evidence that AI demand is creating a more durable memory upcycle rather than simply producing another short-lived period of supply shortages and elevated prices.
Particular attention is likely to be paid to:
Fiscal 2027 revenue and margin expectations
Multi-year customer agreements are also becoming increasingly important because they could give Micron greater visibility over future demand and reduce some of the cyclicality traditionally associated with the memory market.
Capital expenditure will be closely watched
Micron is investing heavily to expand production capacity.
The company spent $7.1bn on capital expenditure in Q3, although this was more than offset by its substantial cash generation. Adjusted free cash flow reached $18.3bn and Micron ended the quarter with $30.2bn of cash, marketable investments and restricted cash.
The investment programme is necessary if Micron is to capture the expected growth in AI-related memory demand.
However, investors will be watching for signs that capital expenditure could eventually create excess capacity. This is particularly important given the memory industry's history of aggressive investment followed by periods of oversupply.
The balance between capacity growth and demand growth could therefore be one of the most important longer-term issues discussed on the earnings call.
Shareholder returns are another potential area of interest.
Micron currently pays a quarterly dividend of $0.15 per share, but the bigger potential catalyst is the company's ability to resume share repurchases.
Restrictions associated with funding received under the US Chips Act have limited Micron's ability to buy back shares. Those restrictions are expected to expire in December 2026, potentially giving management greater flexibility to return excess cash to shareholders.
With cash generation accelerating sharply, investors may look for an indication of how Micron intends to allocate capital once those restrictions expire.
Micron shares: what matters now?
The extraordinary improvement in Micron's fundamentals has already changed the way investors view the company. It is no longer simply a cyclical memory-chip manufacturer waiting for the next upturn in pricing.
AI infrastructure spending has created a powerful new source of demand, while HBM has become strategically important to the semiconductor supply chain.
But that also means expectations are considerably higher.
A strong fourth-quarter result accompanied by bullish fiscal 2027 guidance could reinforce the view that the current memory cycle has further to run. Conversely, signs that HBM demand is slowing, pricing is approaching a peak or capital expenditure is running ahead of demand could raise concerns about the sustainability of current margins.
For those wanting to understand more about how to trade shares in high-growth technology companies where guidance and forward expectations matter as much as headline results, our resources on online trading cover the key concepts in accessible detail.
​Analysts rate Micron as a ‘buy’ with a mean long-term upside target at $1,452.08, around 38% above the company’s current share price (as of 29/09/2026).
​TipRanks attributes a ’10 Outperform’ Smart Score to Micron with a ‘strong buy’ rating.
Technical analysis of the Micron share price
​The Micron Technology share price – up 269% year-to-date – remains in a strong uptrend with the September peak at $1,108.72 remaining in sight. If bettered on a daily chart closing basis, the June all-time high at $1,255 may be back in sight.
​Micron Technology weekly candlestick chart

​For now good support lies between the 9 July-to-9 September highs at $1,042.40-to-$1,011.77 and withstands downside pressure.
​Micron Technology daily candlestick chart
​Only a bearish reversal and fall through the late August low at $887.61 may push the late July low at $737.88 to the fore.
​The bottom line: Micron's September results are likely to be less about whether the company can deliver another record quarter and more about how long the AI-driven memory boom can sustain its exceptional growth and margins.
​With the market already expecting extraordinary numbers, fiscal 2027 guidance, HBM demand and the outlook for memory pricing could prove more important than the headline Q4 results themselves. The key question is whether Micron can turn the current AI-driven surge into a durable, less cyclical earnings cycle.

Micron Stock Outlook: Baird Sets $1,520 Target as MU Eyes $1,600
The Micron stock outlook is still bullish right now, and Wall Street has set a Micron stock price target of $1,500 to $1,600 ahead of fiscal Q4 earnings on September 30. MU closed at $1,053.98 on Monday and traded at $1,069.27 in pre-market at the time of writing. The average MU stock price target of $1,515 points to roughly 44% upside. After the Micron stock 2026 rally of about 269%, will MU stock go up even further? Analysts think it can, as long as AI demand and tight DRAM supply hold up.
Also Read: Micron Earnings: Can MU Stock Beat High Expectations?
Micron Stock in 2026: Price Targets, AI Demand And MU’s Next Move
The Micron stock outlook now comes down to whether AI memory demand keeps earnings high for longer than in past cycles. Shares slipped 2.61% on Monday after OpenAI paused training on some of its AI models, but 36 of the 49 analysts on StockAnalysis still rate Micron a Strong Buy.
Baird, Rosenblatt And TD Cowen Stay Bullish
Baird analyst Tristan Gerra just raised his target to $1,520 from $1,280 and kept an Outperform rating. Baird’s new MU stock price target sits almost exactly on the consensus, and it implies about 44% upside from Monday’s close.
Gerra wrote:
“We are incrementally positive on Micron near- and medium term, owing to 1) the recent surge in agentic AI demand, notably driving CPU demand and which we expect will be ongoing next year; 2) a deceleration in [dynamic random access memory] supply bit growth outlook industrywide for 2027 versus this year; 3) a higher margin profile expected for [high bandwidth memory] next year.”
Rosenblatt’s Kevin Cassidy reiterated a Buy rating with a $1,500 Micron stock price target and expects another “beat-and-raise” on Wednesday. TD Cowen’s Krish Sankar holds a Buy rating with a $1,600 target. Both calls add weight to the Micron stock outlook.
Management has also given the bulls plenty to work with, and that feeds into the Micron stock outlook. For fiscal Q4, Micron guided revenue of $50 billion, plus or minus $1 billion, a gross margin of about 86% and earnings of $31 per share, plus or minus $1. Will MU stock go up once the results are out? That depends on beating those numbers.
Sanjay Mehrotra, Micron’s Chairman, President and CEO, stated:
“Micron’s record fiscal Q3 financial results and even stronger outlook for Q4 reflect the strategic value of memory in the AI era. Micron is investing at record levels in technology, products and supply to address our customers’ rapidly growing demand. We believe our multi-year Strategic Customer Agreements will significantly enhance the durability and predictability of Micron’s strong financial performance.”
A Rerating Could Lift The Micron Stock Outlook
MarketWatch reported that Sankar sees room for a “rerating” of Micron shares. At the time of his call, the stock traded at about 5.8 times forward earnings, and he argued the stock could justify a multiple closer to nine times. That wouldn’t need faster growth, only earnings that stay high for longer, and it’s the thinking behind his $1,600 MU stock price target. A higher multiple alone could brighten the MU stock outlook.
The risks behind these Micron stock 2026 forecasts are real, too, such as faster supply additions, weaker HBM demand and falling memory prices.
So, will MU stock go up from here? Most analysts say yes, and right now the Micron stock outlook depends on whether September 30 proves that strong pricing and margins can last. If it does, the $1,500 to $1,600 stock price target range looks realistic.

Micron stock falls 4% ahead of its Q4 earnings.
Baird raises Micron’s price target to $1,520.
AI demand supports Micron’s DRAM and HBM outlook.
Micron Technology MU stock fell 4% on Thursday as investors weighed rising US Treasury yields and higher crude oil prices ahead of the memory chipmaker’s fiscal fourth-quarter earnings report on Sept. 30.
Despite the decline, Baird raised its price target on Micron to $1,520 from $1,280 while reiterating its outperform rating. The new target implies about 40% upside from Friday’s close.
Baird analyst Tristan Gerra said the firm was “incrementally positive on Micron near- and medium term” because of rising demand for agentic artificial intelligence, slower expected DRAM supply growth across the industry in 2027 and a higher-margin outlook for high-bandwidth memory next year.
Micron shares have risen sharply in 2026 alongside other memory stocks, supported in part by a shortage of memory chips.
The stock is up 279% this year and reached an intraday record of $1,255 on June 25.
AI demand supports Micron’s DRAM outlook
Micron is benefiting from growing demand for high-performance memory as artificial intelligence adoption increases.
AI systems process large amounts of data and require memory with greater capacity and bandwidth, supporting demand for DRAM in AI servers and other high-performance computing systems.
DRAM is expected to be Micron’s biggest growth engine in the fourth quarter.
The Zacks Consensus Estimate puts DRAM revenue at $38.26 billion, representing a 325.8% increase from the year-ago quarter.
The expected growth comes alongside improving conditions in the broader memory market.
The industry had previously faced excess supply, weak pricing, and elevated inventories, but those conditions have improved, resulting in a healthier balance between supply and demand.
The combination of stronger AI demand and improved pricing conditions is expected to support DRAM revenue and profitability in the quarter.
High-bandwidth memory has become another important part of Micron’s AI growth outlook.
AI accelerators use HBM to provide the high memory bandwidth required for increasingly complex workloads.
Micron is mass-producing HBM for NVIDIA’s next-generation AI chips, giving the company exposure to growing demand for AI infrastructure.
HBM supply remains relatively tight, while demand from AI data centres continues to increase.
Micron has also highlighted strong demand for HBM4.
Its HBM4 12-high ramp is progressing faster than the earlier HBM3E 12-high ramp, potentially increasing HBM’s contribution to revenue and profitability over time.
Baird’s Gerra also pointed to a higher margin profile for HBM next year as one of the factors supporting the firm’s positive view of Micron.
NVIDIA, AMD and Marvell partnerships support AI exposure
Micron’s relationships with major semiconductor companies provide exposure to several AI platforms.
NVIDIA has selected Micron as a major HBM supplier for its Blackwell GPUs and Vera Rubin AI platform.
Micron also supplies HBM3E products for Advanced Micro Devices’ Instinct MI350 AI accelerators.
The company is also working with Marvell Technology on advanced memory solutions for AI applications.
Marvell’s focus on custom AI silicon provides another potential avenue for Micron to participate in the expansion of AI infrastructure.
Micron’s fiscal fourth-quarter results are due Wednesday.
LSEG consensus expects earnings to rise 939% year over year. Analysts remain broadly positive, with 46 of 49 analysts tracked by LSEG rating the stock a buy or strong buy.
The average analyst price target implies about 34% upside.
